newsitem.title: USA: USDA - Ryegrass smut muddies Karnal Bunt detection.
newsitem.headline: USDA - Ryegrass smut muddies Karnal Bunt detection.

text.p: The U.S. Agriculture Department said Karnal bunt testing in the Southeast United States has been called into question by the discovery of a ryegrass smut that has spores similiar in size and morphology to the fungus.

"This discovery has complicated identification of Karnal bunt, particularly in areas such as the Southeast, where it is common to plant wheat in combination with various foliages, grasses including ryegrass," USDA's Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service said in its "Karnal bunt update."
It said current DNA testing does not distinguish between the ryegrass smut and Karnal bunt.
USDA is conducting pathogenicity tests to distinguish between the two diseases. The tests are expected to be completed at the end of March.
"We're hoping to have some sort of distinction of what kind of smut we have here," said an APHIS spokeswoman.
A national survey had detected Karnal bunt-like teliospores in grain samples from several counties in Alabama, Florida, Georgia and Tennessee.

APHIS said other than the teliospores, which are the causal agent for the wheat fungus, no other evidence of the Karnal bunt disease had been observed in the Southeast, noting in particular that no bunted kernels had been found.
"No regulatory action will be taken until clear evidence exists that the disease occurs in the Southeast region," it added.
The department began the nationwide survey for Karnal bunt last summer after parts of California, Arizona, Texas and New Mexico were quaratined because of the fungus.
Karnal bunt, also called Stinking Smut, makes wheat smell bad and reduces yields and quality. Many nations refuse to accept wheat that contains the fungus.
USDA persuaded customers to continue to purchase U.S. grain by issuing documents to prove the wheat did not come from an infected area.
